The largest increase in median wealth among black females occurred between 1985 and 1990. During this 5-year period, median composite wealth increased by $2,425.00 (from $175.00 in 1985 to $2,600.00 in 1990, an annualized increase of $485.00/year and a relative growth of 1,385.7%). In contrast, between 1990 and 1996 (a 6-year period), median wealth grew by $1,400.00 (reaching $4,000.00 in 1996, an annualized increase of $233.33/year and a relative growth of 53.8%). 

This growth pattern was driven by black females who were never incarcerated (`ever_jailed == 0`, N = 1,532), whose median wealth grew by $2,688.00 between 1985 ($200.00) and 1990 ($2,888.00) versus $1,112.00 between 1990 and 1996 ($4,000.00). Black females who were ever incarcerated (`ever_jailed == 1`, N = 16) maintained a median wealth of $0.00 across all three survey waves.

payload.hypothesis: The largest increase in median wealth among black females occurred between 1985 and 1990, both in total absolute gain ($2,425.00 vs. $1,400.00) and annualized rate of increase ($485.00/year vs. $233.33/year), driven entirely by non-incarcerated individuals.

Computed cross-sectional medians and individual-level changes across the 1985, 1990, and 1996 composite wealth variables. Calculated absolute, percentage, and annualized rates of change across adjacent survey periods, and evaluated subgroup differences by incarceration status (ever_jailed).
